guides.title: Be ready for emergencies: household checklist
guides.summary: Cabinet Office Be Ready advice: build 3 days of supplies, sign up to the Priority Services Register, make a household plan and prepare your home.
guides.body:
# Be ready for emergencies

From severe weather to cyber attacks, emergencies can disrupt the services you rely on. Being ready for 3 days helps you manage while support reaches those in need.

Here are some simple and effective steps you can take to be ready for emergencies and the disruption they cause. Many of these activities can be helpful across a range of different types of emergency. There are lots of suggestions here that won't cost anything and just take a few minutes to do.

For various reasons, not everyone will be able to take all of the actions in the guidance and some people will only follow a few of the recommended steps. The details below provide basic advice on how to prepare, so you can take the steps that work for you.

> ⚠️ Call **999** if you or someone else is in immediate danger.

## The Be Ready checklist

Being ready for 3 days helps you manage while support reaches those most in need. Doing this is easier than you might think. You could have some of the items at home already.

You don't need to do it all at once. Build up your readiness gradually over time by taking it step by step, and picking up an extra item or two when you can.

1. See what you already have: check your cupboards first to see what essentials you already keep at home.
2. Plan for your household: note down what you still need, remembering items your family relies on, such as medical supplies, baby formula or pet food.
3. Build it gradually: pick up missing items when you can during your regular shopping trips to help spread the cost.
4. Check it regularly: set a reminder every six months to check expiry dates and swap out items that need replacing, or update your kit if your household's needs have changed.
5. Connect with your community: talk to your neighbours about what extra support you might be able to share during an outage, and swap contact details.

## What to keep at home

- Bottled water for 3 days: 3 litres per person per day for drinking. More would be needed for other tasks such as cooking and washing.
- Non-perishable food for 3 days: food with a long shelf life that doesn't need refrigeration or cooking, for example tinned meat, fish or vegetables, dried fruit and nuts. It's best to buy food you'd usually eat.
- Hand sanitiser, wet wipes and bathroom products.
- Torch and spare batteries. Torches are safer than candles.
- Blankets, sleeping bags and warm clothing. Homes can become cold very quickly when the heating goes off.
- FM radio (battery or wind up). For updates during outages, write down frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.
- Charged power bank, to charge phones or compatible medical devices.
- Cash (mix of coins and notes) and cards, in case electronic payments or ATMs are disrupted. The amount of cash you should keep depends on your family's specific needs for essentials.
- Copies of IDs and documents: printed copies of important documents such as passports, birth certificates, insurance policy details and instructions for any medical equipment you rely on.
- Important phone numbers and information: write down contact details of who you'd need to contact in an emergency (including anyone who might need checking on) and a list of any regular medication and doses.
- First aid kit or first aid items, including waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers.
- Essential medication and medical supplies. Always leave enough time to request repeat prescriptions so you have less chance of running out in an emergency. It's important to request prescriptions up to 5 working days before you need your medicine.
- Baby formula. Ready-made or 'ready-to-feed' formula is best, as you may not be able to boil water to make up powdered formula safely.
- Nappies and wipes.
- Pet food and bottled water.

## Be informed

- Sign up for alerts and warnings and find out about different types of hazards and emergencies.
- Find out more about risks in your local area, including checking your flood risk.
- Learn some basic first aid skills. Check online to find free workshops or ask if your employer will pay for a course.
- Check if the place where you work or volunteer has a plan for what you should do if you cannot contact them during an emergency, for example in a power cut.

Find out if you are eligible to sign up to the Priority Services Register (PSR). This lets your electricity, gas and water providers know that you need additional support, including when there is an interruption to your supply. Lots of households are eligible, including those with children under 5. This service is available to customers in England, Scotland and Wales.

## Make a plan

- Use a household emergency plan. Keep this with other important documents such as passports, birth certificates and insurance policies so it's easier to gather them quickly if needed.
- Work out the best escape route from your home if there is a fire, or what you should do if your home floods. If you live with others, including children, discuss this with them.
- Decide on a meeting point with family members in case you cannot return home or contact each other for a period of time. Choose places that are easy to find and open to the public in your community, or you might agree to meet at a family member's home if it is safe to do so.
- Agree on a backup plan with anyone who might need extra support, particularly if they live alone. You could agree that if an outage happens and you cannot call, you or another trusted person they know will visit them in person. Remind them that they should follow the advice of the emergency services if they are asked to evacuate for their safety.
- Speak to the neighbours of anyone you would be worried about in an outage and agree that they will check on them.
- Write down important phone numbers on paper and store them somewhere easy to find in a power cut. Include the phone number to report a power cut (**105** in England, Scotland and Wales and 03457 643643 in Northern Ireland), phone numbers of anyone you would want to contact in an emergency, a list of your regular medication, frequencies of radio stations you use for news updates, and insurance policy details.
- Add emergency contacts or medical information to your mobile phone (often called 'ICE' or 'Medical ID' on smartphones) so that emergency services can access this information without having to unlock your phone with a passcode.
- Check your child's school or other childcare provider has the correct contact numbers for you in case they need to contact you during an emergency.

## Prepare your home

- Set a reminder in your phone or make a note on your calendar to check your smoke alarms at least once a month.
- Know how to turn off your gas, electricity and water. You'll need to turn these off if you have to leave your home due to flooding or for other reasons such as if there's a leak.
- Check the right insurance is in place for your home (or business), for example, flood insurance.
- If you live in a flood risk area, find out more actions you can take to prepare your property.
- You could consider keeping some essential items you might need to take with you if asked to leave your home quickly in a spare bag. You might hear some people call this a 'grab bag'.
- Pack a few essential items in your car boot to make sure you're ready in case of getting stuck in wintry weather. This can include a torch, in-car phone charger, warm clothes and blankets, high-visibility clothing, jump leads, food and drink, and a shovel for snow. It can also be helpful to keep a first aid kit in your car.

## Talk to others

- Talk about this advice and pass on information about the support available. Help your friends, family, neighbours and colleagues to undertake the simple actions, if they can.
- Swap contact details with neighbours and consider creating an instant messaging group or other closed online social network for your street or building. These can be an important source of information and support during an emergency.
- Ask your neighbours if they might have additional support needs during an emergency. They may have additional medical needs, be new to the area, not be able to use the internet or technology well, or not speak or read English well. Talk to them about the help available and how you can support them.
- Make a plan to check in on neighbours if an emergency happens, particularly if the power goes out.
- Talk to children about what to do in an emergency, including how and when to call the emergency services. You can also help them to learn their home address and if possible, a parent or guardian's mobile phone number. Practise these regularly.

guides.title: Flooding: prepare and what to do during a flood
guides.summary: Check flood risk, sign up for flood warnings and make a flood plan, and know exactly what to do when a flood warning or severe flood warning is issued.
guides.body:
# Flooding: prepare and what to do during a flood

## Protect yourself from future flooding

You can:

- check for flooding in the next 5 days
- get flood warnings by text, phone or email
- check your long term flood risk from rivers, the sea, surface water, reservoirs and groundwater (where data is available)

## Make a flood plan

Plan how you'll respond to a flood. You can make a:

- personal flood plan
- community or group flood plan, if you're responsible for an organisation such as a school, hospital, care home or community group
- business flood plan

Keep your flood plan in a safe place with other essential items, for example spare medication, important documents and contact details.

## Find local support

Find out what support is available in your local area before, during and after a flood, for example:

- flood action groups, volunteers who work with local councils and agencies to reduce flood risks and represent local people
- community flood wardens, volunteers who monitor a specific local area and tell residents when flooding is likely to happen
- community hubs, where you can find food, clothing, shelter and advice during a flood

You can find your nearest flood action group, community flood wardens or community hub on social media, on your local council's website, or by contacting the National Flood Forum.

## If you have a disability or need extra help

Ask your local council if you can get extra help during a flood. Ask Floodline to send flood warnings to a friend or relative on your behalf.

Floodline. Telephone: **0345 988 1188**. Textphone: 0345 602 6340. 24-hour service.

## If you get a flood warning

If your area has a flood warning, flooding is expected. To stay safe:

- move your family, pets and important items to safety, for example upstairs or to higher ground
- use flood protection products if you have them, for example flood barriers or air brick covers
- turn off your gas, electricity and water supplies if it's safe to do so
- do not drive through flood water, only move your vehicle to higher ground if it's safe to do so
- follow advice from your local council or the emergency services, you may be asked to evacuate

> ⚠️ Do not touch an electrical switch if you're standing in water.

## If you get a severe flood warning

A severe flood warning means there is a danger to life.

To keep yourself and others safe:

- call **999** if you or someone else is in immediate danger
- leave the area if the emergency services tell you to evacuate
- do not walk, cycle or drive through flood water
- do not put yourself at risk to move vehicles or belongings

## If you need to travel

Do not walk, cycle or drive through flood water. Flood water may contain sewage and hide rubbish, wreckage, uneven roads and pavements or broken drain and manhole covers.

## Get emergency accommodation

If your home is flood damaged and you're not able to live there, contact your local council for help getting emergency accommodation.

## Report a flood or an electrical, gas or sewage problem

To report:

- an electrical hazard or power cut, contact your local electricity company or call **105** (calls are free)
- a gas leak, contact National Gas
- an overflowing sewer, contact your water company

You may need a permit to pump water out of a property. You can ask your local fire brigade for help pumping out water. They might charge a fee and can help you get a permit.

## If you own a riverside property

If you own property next to a watercourse, for example a river, culvert, brook or mill stream, you must:

- maintain river beds and banks
- not obstruct the water flow
- not pollute the water
- protect wildlife

Contact the Environment Agency if you have questions about your responsibilities. Telephone: 03708 506 506, Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm.

guides.title: Power cuts: prepare, stay safe and keep food safe
guides.summary: How to prepare for and get through a power cut: report it on 105, stay warm, and store and cook food safely when the electricity is off.
guides.body:
# Power cuts

Power cuts (or electricity outages) can have a number of causes including severe weather, which can lead to damaged infrastructure, or system faults.

The UK has a resilient electricity system. Most power cuts are short-lived and occur locally, but more widespread and longer outages can happen. These could potentially last several days with regional or, although unlikely, national impacts.

Gas ovens, boilers, heat pumps and your home internet won't work without power. Your mobile phone might stop working if your local mast is in the affected area. Mains water supply to your home could also be disrupted during and after power cuts.

## Prepare for a power cut

- Keep a battery or wind-up torch (and spare batteries) at home. Torches are safer than candles. You probably won't want to use the torch on your mobile phone as this will drain its batteries more quickly.
- Keep at least 3 days' worth of bottled water (3 litres per person per day) and non-perishable food that doesn't need cooking such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables and a tin opener. You should also include ready-made baby formula and pet food if needed.
- If you're eligible, sign up to your energy supplier's Priority Services Register to let them know that you need additional support during a power cut. Lots of households are eligible, including those with children under 5.
- Find out your power load block letter. In the unlikely event of a national energy shortage, emergency power cuts could be scheduled on a rotating area-by-area basis. Each area in GB is assigned a 'load block letter' and would be scheduled to disconnect from the electricity grid for around three hours at a time.
- Keep a small amount of cash for essential purchases if electronic payments or ATMs are disrupted.
- Write down the phone number to report a power cut. This is **105** in England, Scotland and Wales and 03457 643643 in Northern Ireland. You can also save the number in your mobile phone.
- Keep a battery or wind-up radio (and spare batteries) at home. There might be updates communicated by radio during a power cut. Write down on paper the frequencies of any local or national radio stations you use for news updates.
- If your only way of making emergency calls is through a landline phone, or if you have a telecare kit connected to your landline, contact your landline provider to understand whether your phone will work during a power cut. If your landline will not work during a power cut, your landline provider might offer you a free solution (such as a back-up battery unit), for a minimum of one hour, that would enable you to call the emergency services during a power cut if you needed to.
- If you have a personal alarm (also known as telecare devices) or other connected equipment monitoring your health such as diabetes sensors, speak to your device provider or manufacturer to understand how they will function during a power cut.

## During a power cut

- Visit your local network operator's website to report a power cut and track updates when there's a problem. If you're unable to report the power cut online, call 105 for free in England, Wales and Scotland and 03457 643643 in Northern Ireland.
- Keep away from hazards such as power lines. Electricity at high voltages can jump gaps with no warning.
- Turn off items such as irons, ovens, electric fires and fryers. Unplug your TV and PC as they can be damaged if there is a surge when power goes back on.
- Keep warm by using blankets and layered clothing. Keep doors of unused rooms closed and close curtains to keep the heat in. Older adults, babies and young children, and people with long-term health problems are most likely to become ill if they get too cold.
- Check in on neighbours and, if you are able, offer to share blankets, clothing or other supplies such as food. You can also pass on any important information you might have received about the power cut, such as when the power is expected to go back on.
- In a power cut your TV or internet might not be working. To get news updates use a battery or wind-up radio to search for stations that are still broadcasting. Try FM and digital modes.
- Keep fridges and freezer doors closed, as this will ensure they stay cold for several hours.

> ⚠️ If you don't have back-up power to your landline phone and have a life-threatening emergency, you should attempt to call **999** or 112 using a mobile. Emergency calls automatically 'roam' onto all available networks.

## Food safety in a power cut

If a power cut has affected your home and your electricity supply has been cut off, it's important you continue to store and prepare food safely. If the power outage is for less than 4 hours this is unlikely to impact the safety of food in chilled or frozen storage.

Your fridge should stay cold for up to 4 hours. The food in your freezer should stay frozen for up to 48 hours in a full freezer (or 24 hours if it's half full), but these are estimates.

In normal circumstances, fridges should be kept at 5°C or below, but in power cuts, food can be stored in fridges at temperatures under 8°C. If the temperature rises to 8°C and above, you should eat food that normally requires refrigeration within 4 hours first.

If the weather is cold (below 8°C), you can store food outside. Store food in clean dry conditions, out of direct sunlight and protect it from animals. You should use a sealed box to prevent contamination and tampering.

Food that is normally stored at ambient temperature will continue to be safe to eat. Some foods such as tinned foods will be safe to eat without heating through. Consider eating these foods only after you have eaten perishable foods that require chilled storage.

## Cooking and eating during a power cut

Electric or induction cookers will not work during a power cut, but gas cookers may continue to function. If available, you can also cook food and heat water for food preparation and cleaning using a camping stove, barbecue, or bottled gas stove.

> ⚠️ Check the manufacturer's instructions for safe use of these appliances, as most are designed for outdoor use only.

Cooking with these appliances can take longer than conventional cooking, so you need to take extra care that food is steaming hot and cooked through.

Wash your hands before touching food and clean work surfaces and utensils. You can use alcohol-based hand sanitiser for cleaning your hands or antibacterial sprays or wipes for surfaces and utensils if the water supply is also affected. Continue to keep raw and cooked foods separate to avoid cross-contamination.

Chilled foods first need to be kept below 8°C to keep them safe. If the fridge temperature has reached 8°C or above, these foods should be discarded after 4 hours (unless the power is restored within 4 hours) as they may not be safe to eat.

To keep food safe and reduce food waste, use foods in the following order:

1. foods that need refrigeration
2. defrosted frozen food that doesn't need cooking
3. room-temperature perishable food
4. room-temperature canned, bottled, and dried food

Some people are at increased risk of food poisoning, including young children, pregnant women, older people and people with an underlying health condition. For these people:

- wash hands, surfaces and utensils often to prevent cross contamination
- be cautious with high-risk foods like deli meats and smoked fish
- make sure food is steaming hot before being eaten
- don't consume expired or spoiled food, check use-by dates

To prepare baby formula safely, you will need to be able to boil water and follow the normal safety procedures. If you are not able to boil water, another option could be to use ready-to-use infant formula.

## If you need extra support

If you use medical equipment that requires a power supply, make a plan with your care provider and clinical care teams now about what will happen in a power cut. The plan should set out what action you, or someone you care for, needs to take and who to contact if there's a power outage.

The Priority Services Register is a free service to help people who have additional needs. Wherever possible, you will receive advanced notice of scheduled power cuts. If you rely on your energy supply for medical reasons, your network operator can tell you about planned power cuts. You can also get priority support in an emergency.

guides.title: Hot and cold weather: staying safe
guides.summary: UKHSA advice on coping with hot weather (heat exhaustion, heatstroke, cooling your home) and keeping warm and well in cold weather.
guides.body:
# Hot and cold weather: staying safe

## Hot weather: actions to stay safe

Anyone can become unwell if they get too hot. However, some people are at higher risk of becoming seriously unwell.

- If you are going to do a physical activity (for example exercise or walking the dog), plan to do these during times of the day when it is cooler such as the early morning or the evening.
- Keep your home cool by closing windows and curtains in rooms that face the sun.
- Drink plenty of fluids and limit your alcohol intake.
- Check on family, friends and neighbours who may be at higher risk of becoming unwell, and if you are at higher risk, ask them to do the same for you.
- Try to avoid direct sunlight, especially between 11am and 3pm when UV levels are highest.
- If you are going out during this time, cover up with suitable clothing, wear a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses, seek shade and apply sunscreen liberally and re-apply frequently.

## People at higher risk in hot weather

- older people aged 65 years and over
- babies and young children aged 5 years and under
- people with underlying health conditions particularly heart problems, breathing problems, dementia, diabetes, kidney disease, Parkinson's disease, or mobility problems
- pregnant women
- people on certain medications
- people who are already ill and dehydrated
- people who live alone and may be unable to care for themselves

You should continue taking all of your prescribed medicines unless advised not to by a medical professional. If you have any health concerns, please call **NHS 111**. Some medications need to be stored below 25°C or in the fridge, following the storage instructions on the packaging.

## Heat exhaustion and heatstroke

Heat exhaustion occurs when the body overheats and cannot cool down. Heat exhaustion does not usually need emergency medical attention if you cool down within 30 minutes. If you do not take action to cool down, heat exhaustion can lead to heatstroke.

Common symptoms of heat exhaustion include tiredness, weakness, feeling faint, headache, muscle cramps, feeling or being sick, heavy sweating and intense thirst.

Heatstroke is where the body is no longer able to cool down and the body temperature becomes dangerously high. Common symptoms of heatstroke include confusion, lack of co-ordination, fast heartbeat, fast breathing or shortness of breath, hot skin that is not sweating, and seizures.

> ⚠️ Heatstroke is a medical emergency. If you think someone has heatstroke you should dial **999** and then try to cool them down.

To cool down if you or someone else has symptoms of heat exhaustion:

1. Move to a cooler place such as a room with air conditioning or somewhere in the shade, and avoid direct sunlight.
2. Remove all unnecessary clothing like a jacket or socks.
3. Drink cool water, a sports or rehydration drink, or eat cold and water rich foods like ice-lollies.
4. Apply cool water by spray or sponge to exposed skin. Using cold packs wrapped in a cloth and put under the armpits or on the neck can also help.

You should start to cool down and feel better within 30 minutes. If you are concerned about symptoms, or they are worsening, seek medical advice by contacting NHS 111. In an emergency, or if you think someone has heatstroke, dial 999.

## Keeping your home cool

- Close blinds and curtains on windows that are exposed to direct sunlight during the day.
- Close external shutters or shades if you have them.
- Move to a cooler part of the house, especially for sleeping.
- Open windows (if it is safe to) when the air feels cooler outside than inside, for example at night, and try to get air flowing through your home.
- Use electric fans if the air temperature is below 35°C, but do not aim the fan directly at your body as this can lead to dehydration.
- Check that any heating is turned off.
- Turn off lights and electrical equipment that are not in use.

Public buildings such as places of worship, local libraries or supermarkets may be cooler than your home. If they are nearby consider visiting one of these as a way of cooling down.

## Cold weather: who is at risk

Whilst exposure to cold weather can affect anyone, some people are particularly at risk. These include:

- older people (aged 65 years and over)
- people with long-term health conditions such as cardiovascular or respiratory disease, or a mental health condition
- pregnant women
- young children (particularly those aged 5 and under)
- people who live alone and may be unable to care for themselves
- people living in deprived circumstances

During cold weather, people may also use malfunctioning or inappropriate appliances to heat their homes. This can increase the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning. When a house is damp as well as cold, mould is more likely to occur. This can increase the risk of illness, especially from asthma.

## Keep your home warm

You should heat your home to a temperature that is comfortable for you. Low indoor temperatures can have a serious impact on your health, especially if you have medical conditions or are older.

- Try to heat rooms you spend a lot of time in, such as the living room or bedroom, to at least **18°C**.
- Try to reduce draughts; you can fit draft excluders around doors cheaply.
- Keep your bedroom windows closed at night.
- Wear several layers of thinner clothing; this could keep you warmer than one thicker layer.

## Look after yourself and others

- Try not to sit still for more than an hour or so.
- If you find it difficult to move about, stretching your arms and legs can also help keep you warm.
- When out and about, wear shoes with good grip to avoid slips and falls on slippery or icy surfaces.
- If bad weather is forecast, plan ahead and check that you've got enough medication and food in case it's harder to leave the house.

Other people around you, particularly older neighbours, family friends and neighbours, may need extra support during cold weather. To support others you can:

- keep in touch with them and ask whether they are feeling unwell, or whether they need any practical help
- if bad weather is forecast, see if they need any help stocking up on food and medication
- if you are worried about someone else's health, contact your local pharmacist, your GP or NHS 111, who will all be able to offer advice and support

> ⚠️ If you think someone may have hypothermia, contact **NHS 111** for further assessment, and in an emergency dial **999**. Typical signs that someone may be suffering from hypothermia include shivering, slow breathing, tiredness or confusion, and pale, cold skin.

## Prepare your home for winter

- Have your heating and cooking appliances checked by a Gas Safe registered engineer to make sure they are working safely.
- Have a carbon monoxide alarm (EN 50291 compliant) fitted.
- Have things like boiler flues and chimneys checked for blockages and cleared if necessary.
- Insulate water pipes to prevent them from freezing in cold weather.
- Contact your water and power suppliers to see if you can be on the Priority Services Register, a free support service that helps people in vulnerable situations.

If you are worried about your health or feeling down, contact your local pharmacist, NHS 111 or your GP, who will all be able to offer advice and support. In an emergency dial 999.

guides.title: What to do after a flood
guides.summary: How to clean up safely after a flood: return home, insurance claims, disposing of contaminated items, and food and water safety.
guides.body:
# What to do after a flood

Check with the emergency services that it's safe to return to your property.

> ⚠️ Do not turn on your water, gas or electricity. Get your utilities company or a qualified engineer to check they are safe before turning them back on.

## If you rent your home

Your landlord is responsible for repairs to your home if you've got flood damage.

## Contact your insurance company

Contact your insurance company to start your claim. They'll tell you what to do next.

If you do not have insurance, contact your local council if you need emergency housing because of flooding. They may also be able to tell you about grants or charities that can help with repairs to your property.

## Clearing up and making repairs

Before you start clearing up:

- take photos of any damage and the flood water line
- speak to your insurance company about what you can move and throw away

Flood water may contain sewage and hide rubbish, wreckage, uneven roads and pavements or broken drain and manhole covers.

You can put most things in the bin as long as they're not polluted by sewage or chemicals. Contact your local council if you need skips or extra rubbish collections. If you have used sandbags, check with your local council about how to dispose of them.

Contact the environmental health department at your local council to get rid of things polluted by chemicals or sewage. The council will tell you how to dispose of them as hazardous waste.

## Food and water safety

After a flood, you can stay healthy by:

- not using tap water if you notice a change in the colour, taste or smell. Contact your water company if this happens.
- not eating food that's touched flood water
- throwing away food from a fridge if the electricity has been off for more than 4 hours
- throwing away food from a freezer if the electricity has been off for more than 24 hours

## Get help and support

If you need information and advice, contact Floodline. Telephone: **0345 988 1188**. Textphone: 0345 602 6340. 24-hour service.

If you need support with your mental health:

- speak to your friends and family or your doctor
- check the NHS website to find where you can get urgent help for mental health
- contact the Samaritans to talk to a trained volunteer anonymously for free, confidential support 24 hours a day

You may be able to get financial support from your local council after a flood. Contact your local council to find out if support is available.

## Prepare for future floods

Find out what you can do to protect your property from flooding in the future, and what insurance you can get if you own or rent your property.

guides.title: Storms: before, during and after
guides.summary: What to do before, during and after a storm, including securing your property, staying safe in high winds and dealing with downed power lines.
guides.body:
# Storms

Storms can lead to disruption to power, internet and phone networks, fallen trees and flooded infrastructure. Storms can also cause issues with travel (including planes, cars and trains). You should pay extra attention to advice and warnings when a storm is named by the Met Office (for example, Storm Arwen), as these storms are more likely to bring the biggest impacts.

Strong winds can cause large waves that flood the coast, and can drive storm surges, where seawater is pushed towards the coast. Sometimes storms can lead to severe inland flooding from rain, or along coasts from storm surges overtopping flood defences.

## Before a storm or if one is forecast

- Check the weather forecasts, or download the Met Office Weather Forecast app where you can create alerts for your area. Pay particular attention to any National Severe Weather Warnings covering your area, and act on any advice issued.
- Make sure you know who your power provider is and how to contact them if you have a power outage.
- Charge mobile phones, power banks and any back-up batteries for medical equipment in case there is a power cut.
- Limit travel as much as you can. If you need to make a journey, allow extra time and check for the latest advice from your travel operator ahead of time, and adhere to 'Do Not Travel' notices.
- Check on those in your community who might need extra help and offer practical support (for example help obtaining food or medication) if possible.
- Secure loose objects such as ladders, trampolines, garden furniture, toys or play equipment, or anything else that could be blown around in high winds.
- Close and securely fasten doors and windows, particularly those on the side of the building facing the wind, and large doors such as those on garages. Loft trap doors should be closed and secured with bolts, particularly if your roof pitch is less than 30°. If the house is fitted with storm shutters over the windows then ensure that these are closed and fastened.
- Park vehicles in a garage, if available. Otherwise keep them clear of buildings, trees, walls and fences.
- If your chimney stacks are tall and in poor condition, move any beds away from areas directly below them.
- Check if schools and colleges are planning to close, and make alternative childcare arrangements if necessary.
- Be aware that thunderstorm activity has been linked to increases in people reporting symptoms of asthma and seeking medical attention for issues with their breathing.

## During a storm

- Try not to go outside unless absolutely necessary. If you do go outside, try not to walk or shelter close to buildings, fences, boundary walls and trees. If possible, enter and leave your house through doors on the sheltered side, closing them behind you.
- Do not go outside to repair damage to your property while the storm is in progress.
- Open internal doors only as needed, and close them behind you.
- If you need to drive, take care on exposed routes such as bridges, or high open roads, delay your journey or find alternative routes if possible. Slow down and be aware of side winds, particularly if you are towing or are a high sided vehicle.

> ⚠️ If you see power lines that have been brought down or damaged, keep as far away as possible. Electricity at high voltages can jump gaps with no warning.

## After a storm

- Be careful not to touch any electrical or telephone cables that have been blown down or are still hanging.
- Do not walk too close to walls, buildings and trees as they could have been weakened.
- Make sure that any neighbours or relatives who might need additional support are safe and help them make arrangements for any repairs.
